Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

answer:
ARGUMENT

**A Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case; Plausible Factual Allegations of Discrimination Suffice.**

Rule 8(a)(2) requires only "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief." Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2). To survive a motion under Rule 12(b)(6), a complaint must plead enough factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007). In a discrimination case, that standard does not require a prima facie case. It does require facts from which discrimination may plausibly be inferred.

**A. The prima facie case is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement.**

The framework of *McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green*, 411 U.S. 792 (1973), allocates the order of proof. The Supreme Court has therefore held that the prima facie case "is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). Requiring a plaintiff to plead it would impose a heightened standard that Rule 8(a) does not contain, particularly because direct evidence uncovered in discovery may make the framework unnecessary. *Id.* at 511–12. *Twombly* did not retreat from that rule; it distinguished *Swierkiewicz* and disclaimed any requirement of heightened fact pleading. 550 U.S. at 569–70.

The Fourth Circuit agrees. A discrimination plaintiff need not plead facts establishing a prima facie case to survive dismissal. *McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp., State Highway Admin.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015); *see Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 647–48 (4th Cir. 2017) (applying this principle to a race-discrimination claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and reversing dismissal). A motion that faults a complaint merely for failing to establish each *McDonnell Douglas* element, such as by identifying a specific comparator, therefore asks the wrong question.

**B. The complaint must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.**

Freedom from pleading a prima facie case does not excuse a plaintiff from pleading facts. The complaint must allege facts that plausibly satisfy the elements of the statutory claim, including that the employer acted because of a protected characteristic. *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585–86; *see Bass v. E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co.*, 324 F.3d 761, 764–65 (4th Cir. 2003) (plaintiff need not prove her case in the complaint but must allege facts supporting her claim). Labels, conclusions, and bare assertions are not enough. *Nemet Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc.*, 591 F.3d 250, 255 (4th Cir. 2009). Thus, the court has affirmed dismissal where allegations of race discrimination were conclusory. *Coleman v. Md. Ct. of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190–91 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd sub nom. Coleman v. Ct. of Appeals of Md.*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012); *see McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585–88 (affirming dismissal where the allegation that the employer preferred other candidates because of race and sex rested on speculation).

Plausibility, however, is not probability. *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678. The court accepts well-pleaded facts as true and draws reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. *Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd.*, 822 F.3d 159, 165–66 (4th Cir. 2016). A plaintiff need not show that relief is probable or that alternative explanations are less likely; she need only move her claim across the line from conceivable to plausible. *Houck v. Substitute Tr. Servs., Inc.*, 791 F.3d 473, 484 (4th Cir. 2015). Nor may a court dismiss merely because the defendant offers a competing explanation for its conduct. *See SD3, LLC v. Black & Decker (U.S.) Inc.*, 801 F.3d 412, 425 (4th Cir. 2015). An employer's asserted nondiscriminatory reason is ordinarily tested on evidence, not resolved on the pleadings.

The question, then, is not whether Plaintiff has proved discrimination or established a prima facie case. It is whether the facts alleged, taken as true and read together, permit a reasonable inference that Defendant discriminated against Plaintiff. If they do, the motion to dismiss must be denied.
